claims.claim: Construction costs (labor + materials + subcontractors) account for 64.4% of the average US new-home sale price, with the rest going to the lot, financing, commissions, overhead, and builder profit.
claims.episode_span: still keeps the total material floor well below the finished construction cost reported in most U.S. and Canadian markets
claims.source_title: Cost of Constructing a Home in 2024 - Eye On Housing (NAHB)
claims.supporting_quote: Construction costs account for 64.4% of the average price of a home, according to NAHB’s most recent Cost of Construction Survey . In 2022, the share was 3.6 points lower, at 60.8%.

claims.claim: Building a new US single-family home takes months of calendar time - on average 9.1 months, including 1.4 months just for authorization/permitting before construction starts.
claims.episode_span: Those inspection and permitting cycles can stretch weeks or months, during which interest accrues on land loans and construction financing.
claims.source_title: Single-Family Homes Are Built Faster in 2024 - Eye On Housing (NAHB)
claims.supporting_quote: On average, it now takes 9.1 months from start to finish. That includes 1.4 months for authorization to start construction and another 7.6 months to finish construction.

claims.claim: Regulatory stringency and labor shortage lengthen home construction timelines - build times are about two months longer than in 2015.
claims.episode_span: Builders and buyers alike have come to treat this price level as normal because the industry has optimized within the existing on-site model rather than questioning its underlying sequence.
claims.source_title: Single-Family Homes Are Built Faster in 2024 - Eye On Housing (NAHB)
claims.supporting_quote: However, it is still almost two months longer than the average completion time in 2015. The extra time is largely attributable to a more stringent regulatory environment, elevated mortgage rates, and a shortage of skilled labor.

claims.claim: Federal law caps commercial vehicle width at 102 inches (2.6 m) on the National Network of highways, constraining the size of factory-built modules that travel by road.
claims.episode_span: Transport of finished components is constrained by highway limits on module width and height, so even factory-built sections must be designed around those envelopes.
claims.source_title: Federal Size Regulations for Commercial Motor Vehicles - FHWA
claims.supporting_quote: The Surface Transportation Assistance Act (STAA) of 1982 extended the same width requirement of 102 inches to commercial trucks. At the same time, the STAA expanded the highway network on which the Federal width provision applied from the Interstate to the National Network (NN) of highways.

claims.claim: Stick/light-frame construction with standardized dimensional lumber is the dominant residential construction method in North America.
claims.episode_span: Conventional residential construction still follows a long-established sequence of site preparation, foundation work, stick framing or masonry, mechanical rough-ins, and sequential finishing trades, each performed largely outdoors and exposed to weather.
claims.supporting_quote: Light-frame construction using standardized dimensional lumber has become the dominant construction method in North America and Australia due to the economy of the method; use of minimal structural material allows builders to enclose a large area at minimal cost while achieving a wide variety of architectural styles.

claims.claim: Factory-made wall and floor panels are increasingly used because they save time and cost versus on-site framing.
claims.episode_span: entire wall, floor, and roof sections can be completed inside a weather-protected factory
claims.supporting_quote: The use of factory-made walls and floors has shown an increase in popularity due to the time-saving and cost-efficiency.
